gloss: The outer form of something, seen as an outline.
examples: The cookies were cut in the *shape* of stars.
Draw three different *shapes* on the board.
That cloud has a funny *shape*.

gloss: A perfectly round flat shape.
examples: The kids sat in a *circle* on the rug.
She drew a *circle* around the right answer.
Cut the dough into small *circles*.

gloss: A shape with four equal straight sides and four right angles.
examples: Fold the paper into a *square*.
The quilt is made of hundreds of colored *squares*.
Move your piece three *squares* forward.

gloss: A flat shape with three straight sides and three angles.
examples: Cut each sandwich into two *triangles*.
The roof forms a perfect *triangle*.
A *triangle* has angles that add up to 180 degrees.

gloss: A flat shape with four right angles and opposite sides of equal length.
examples: The screen is a wide *rectangle*.
Draw a *rectangle* twice as long as it is tall.
Most doors are simple *rectangles*.

gloss: A shape like a slightly flattened circle, similar to an egg.
examples: The mirror is a tall *oval*.
She has a narrow face, almost a perfect *oval*.
The track is made of two straight lines and two *ovals*.

gloss: A regular oval curve, like a circle seen from an angle.
examples: The planet moves in an *ellipse* around the sun.
He stretched the circle into an *ellipse*.
The graph showed two overlapping *ellipses*.

gloss: Half of a circle.
examples: The chairs were arranged in a *semicircle*.
Cut the pita in half to make two *semicircles*.
The window above the door is a small *semicircle*.

gloss: A flat shape with six straight sides.
examples: Each cell in a honeycomb is a tiny *hexagon*.
The floor tiles are white *hexagons*.
A stop sign is an octagon, not a *hexagon*.

gloss: A flat shape with five straight sides.
examples: A soccer ball is covered with *pentagons* and hexagons.
Draw a *pentagon* with equal sides.
The garden plot is shaped like a *pentagon*.

gloss: A flat shape with eight straight sides.
examples: A stop sign is a red *octagon*.
The gazebo is built as an *octagon*.
The kids learned to draw *octagons* in art class.

gloss: Any flat shape made of three or more straight sides.
examples: A triangle is the simplest *polygon*.
The video game renders thousands of *polygons* per second.
Name each *polygon* by its number of sides.

gloss: A flat shape with four equal sides and angles that are not right angles.
examples: A *rhombus* looks like a squashed square.
The kite is shaped like a *rhombus*.
Draw two *rhombuses* side by side.
contrast: The h is silent: RAHM-bus. The plural is usually rhombuses, but the Latin plural rhombi (RAHM-by) also appears in math books.

gloss: A flat four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides.
examples: The lampshade is shaped like a *trapezoid*.
Find the area of the *trapezoid*.
The flower bed was laid out in two *trapezoids*.
contrast: In American English this shape is a trapezoid; in British English it is a trapezium.

gloss: A perfectly round solid object, like a ball.
examples: The earth is not a perfect *sphere*.
The lamp is a frosted glass *sphere*.
We made *spheres* out of clay.

gloss: A solid shape with six equal square faces.
examples: Drop two *cubes* of ice in the glass.
The box is a perfect *cube*.
Cut the cheese into small *cubes*.

gloss: A solid shape with a round base that narrows to a point at the top.
examples: Orange *cones* blocked off the lane.
Roll the paper into a *cone*.
The mountain rises in a near-perfect *cone*.

gloss: A solid shape with straight sides and two equal circular ends.
examples: A soup can is a *cylinder*.
The engine has four *cylinders*.
Measure the height of the *cylinder*.

gloss: A solid shape with a flat base and triangular sides meeting at a point.
examples: The kids stacked the blocks into a *pyramid*.
The chart is shaped like a *pyramid*.
We built two paper *pyramids* for the science fair.

gloss: A solid glass shape that splits light into colors, or any solid with matching flat ends.
examples: A *prism* breaks sunlight into a rainbow.
The teacher passed around a glass *prism*.
Both *prisms* have triangular ends.

gloss: A thin flat round object or shape.
examples: The moon was a pale *disk* in the sky.
Slice the carrots into thin *disks*.
A metal *disk* covers the drain.
contrast: Americans spell the shape and the computer part disk; disc is kept mainly for music and video discs, as in compact disc.

gloss: A long thin mark on a surface.
examples: Draw a straight *line* from corner to corner.
Write your name on the dotted *line*.
The parking *lines* had faded away.

gloss: A very small round mark.
examples: Her dress is navy with white *dots*.
From the plane the cars looked like tiny *dots*.
Put a *dot* over the i.

gloss: An exact spot, or the sharp end of something.
examples: Mark the *point* where the two lines cross.
The pencil has a very sharp *point*.
Connect the *points* with a ruler.

gloss: A small round mark of a different color from what is around it.
examples: There is a grease *spot* on your tie.
The puppy is white with brown *spots*.
I got a coffee *spot* on the rug.

gloss: A long narrow band of color.
examples: His shirt has thin blue *stripes*.
A yellow *stripe* runs down the middle of the road.
Zebras have black and white *stripes*.

gloss: A line that bends smoothly without any sharp angles.
examples: Slow down before the *curve* in the road.
The chair follows the *curve* of your back.
The graph shows two rising *curves*.

gloss: A curved line that forms part of a circle.
examples: The ball rose in a high *arc* over the fence.
Draw an *arc* with the compass.
The sprinkler sprayed water in wide *arcs*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like ark, the boat in the flood story.

gloss: A place where something turns or curves.
examples: The cabin is just past the *bend* in the river.
There is a sharp *bend* in the pipe.
Take the next two *bends* slowly.

gloss: A shape made when a line curves around and crosses itself.
examples: Make a *loop* with the shoelace.
Her handwriting is full of fancy *loops*.
The roller coaster does a full *loop*.

gloss: A curve that winds around a center point, getting wider or tighter.
examples: The staircase climbs in a tight *spiral*.
A snail shell is a natural *spiral*.
She doodled little *spirals* in the margin.

gloss: A length of something wound into a series of rings.
examples: A *coil* of rope hung by the door.
The heating *coils* glowed red.
He unwound the *coil* of wire.

gloss: A bend or turn in something long and thin.
examples: The path has more *twists* than I remembered.
Give the wire one more *twist*.
There is a *twist* in the cord behind the desk.

gloss: A line that turns sharply left and right again and again.
examples: The trail climbs the hill in a *zigzag*.
Her sweater has red *zigzags* across the front.
Lightning cut a bright *zigzag* through the clouds.

gloss: A shape made of one line crossing another.
examples: Mark the spot with a *cross*.
She wears a small silver *cross*.
There were two white *crosses* painted on the door.

gloss: A sign shaped like a line with a point at one end, used to show direction.
examples: Follow the green *arrow* to baggage claim.
He drew an *arrow* pointing to the error.
Yellow *arrows* mark the detour.

gloss: The space between two lines that meet, measured in degrees.
examples: The ladder leans at a steep *angle*.
A square has four right *angles*.
Cut the board at a 45-degree *angle*.

gloss: One of the flat surfaces or straight edges that form a shape.
examples: A triangle has three *sides*.
Write on one *side* of the paper only.
The box is dented on the left *side*.

gloss: The outer line or border where something ends.
examples: Careful, the *edge* of that paper is sharp.
He sat on the *edge* of the bed.
Sand the rough *edges* smooth.

gloss: The lowest part of a shape or object, which it stands on.
examples: The lamp has a heavy metal *base*.
Measure the *base* of the triangle.
Both statues have marble *bases*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like bass, the low musical part or instrument.

gloss: The outside or top layer of something.
examples: Wipe the *surface* before you paint it.
Leaves floated on the *surface* of the pond.
Clean all the kitchen *surfaces*.

gloss: A completely flat surface that goes on in every direction.
examples: The two lines lie in the same *plane*.
Cut the block along a horizontal *plane*.
The drawing shows three intersecting *planes*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like plain, meaning simple or ordinary; plane is also the short word for airplane.

gloss: The amount of flat space a shape covers.
examples: Find the *area* of the rectangle.
The rug covers most of the floor *area*.
Compare the *areas* of the two circles.

gloss: The total length of the outer edge of a shape or piece of land.
examples: Add up all four sides to get the *perimeter*.
A fence runs around the *perimeter* of the field.
The two shapes have equal *perimeters*.

gloss: A straight line through the center of a circle from one side to the other.
examples: The pipe is two inches in *diameter*.
Measure the *diameter* of the lid.
The two pans have different *diameters*.

gloss: The distance all the way around a circle.
examples: Wrap the tape around the trunk to get its *circumference*.
The *circumference* is a little over three times the diameter.
We compared the *circumferences* of the two balls.

gloss: One of the parts something is divided into.
examples: Draw a straight line *segment* between the two points.
Peel the orange and separate the *segments*.
Each *segment* of the chart is a different color.
contrast: The noun is SEG-munt; the verb, to segment, is often seg-MENT.

gloss: A measurement of length, width, or height.
examples: Give me the *dimensions* of the room.
Length is one *dimension*, height is another.
The box has the same *dimensions* as mine.

gloss: The size relationship between the parts of something.
examples: The head is out of *proportion* with the body.
The room has pleasing *proportions*.
Keep the same *proportion* when you enlarge the photo.

gloss: The quality of having two halves that match exactly.
examples: A butterfly wing shows perfect *symmetry*.
The building is admired for its *symmetry*.
There is no *symmetry* in that pattern at all.

gloss: A pattern of straight lines crossing to form squares.
examples: The city is laid out on a *grid*.
Draw a *grid* of nine squares.
Photos are arranged in neat *grids* on the page.

gloss: The point where two lines or roads cross.
examples: Turn left at the next *intersection*.
Mark the *intersection* of the two lines.
There are traffic lights at both *intersections*.

gloss: The line that shows the outer shape of something.
examples: He traced the *outline* of his hand.
I could just make out the *outline* of the mountains.
Color inside the *outlines*.

gloss: A dark shape seen against a lighter background.
examples: The trees were black *silhouettes* against the sunset.
I recognized his *silhouette* in the doorway.
The dress has a slim *silhouette*.
contrast: Spelled with a silent h and a French ending: say sil-oo-ET.

gloss: The outline or curved shape of a surface.
examples: The seat follows the *contours* of your body.
The map shows the *contours* of the hillside.
Sunlight brought out every *contour* of the rock.

gloss: The shape of a face or object seen from the side.
examples: The coin shows the president in *profile*.
She has a lovely *profile*.
The artist sketched both *profiles*.

gloss: The shape of a person's body.
examples: She has kept her *figure* for years.
A tall *figure* appeared at the end of the hall.
Two dark *figures* moved across the yard.
contrast: Americans say FIG-yur; the British say FIG-uh, with no y sound.

gloss: The blank space along the edge of a page.
examples: The teacher wrote a note in the *margin*.
Leave a one-inch *margin* on both sides.
The *margins* are too narrow to read comfortably.

gloss: The outer edge of something round.
examples: There is lipstick on the *rim* of the glass.
The ball rolled around the *rim* and dropped in.
He polished the chrome *rims* on his truck.

gloss: A long narrow cut in a surface.
examples: Rainwater runs down the *groove* in the tile.
The record has fine *grooves*.
Slide the panel into the *groove*.

gloss: A line made in cloth or paper by folding or crushing it.
examples: Iron the *crease* out of the shirt.
The map has a *crease* right across the city.
His pants had sharp *creases* down the front.

gloss: A part where something is bent over onto itself.
examples: Press down along the *fold*.
The curtain hangs in soft *folds*.
Open the letter at the *fold*.

gloss: A small V-shaped cut in an edge or surface.
examples: He cut a *notch* in the stick to mark the day.
Tighten the belt one *notch*.
There are small *notches* along the ruler.

gloss: A hollow place in a surface where it has been hit.
examples: There is a *dent* in the car door.
The can has a big *dent* in the side.
Small *dents* covered the old toolbox.

gloss: A raised round part on an otherwise flat surface.
examples: Slow down, there is a *bump* in the road.
He has a *bump* on his forehead.
The wall is covered with little *bumps* of dried paint.

gloss: An empty space between two things.
examples: Cold air comes in through the *gap* under the door.
There is a *gap* between his two front teeth.
Fill the *gaps* with caulk.

gloss: A thin line where something is broken but not in pieces.
examples: There is a *crack* in the windshield.
Weeds grow up through the *cracks* in the sidewalk.
A hairline *crack* runs across the plate.

gloss: A rounded swelling that sticks out from a flat surface.
examples: There was a strange *bulge* in his coat pocket.
The wall has a slight *bulge* near the floor.
Water damage left *bulges* in the ceiling.

gloss: A design of shapes or colors that repeats.
examples: The wallpaper has a floral *pattern*.
I like the tile, but not the *pattern*.
The store sells fabric in dozens of *patterns*.

gloss: A colored design printed onto cloth.
examples: She wore a summer dress in a bright *print*.
Animal *prints* are back in style.
The curtains are a small floral *print*.

gloss: A pattern of crossing colored stripes forming squares.
examples: He always wears a red flannel *plaid*.
The blanket is a soft green *plaid*.
The store had *plaids* in every color.
contrast: Spelled with ai but pronounced PLAD, rhyming with sad.

gloss: One of a pattern of evenly spaced round dots on cloth.
examples: Her blouse is covered in white *polka dots*.
I bought a red dress with black *polka dots*.
Each *polka dot* is about the size of a dime.
contrast: In American speech the l is usually silent here: POH-kuh dot, not POHL-kuh.

gloss: A board or pattern of alternating light and dark squares.
examples: The kitchen floor is a black and white *checkerboard*.
He set up the *checkerboard* on the porch.
The quilt is made of two *checkerboards* sewn together.
contrast: American spelling; the British write chequerboard.

gloss: A twisting curved pattern or movement.
examples: The ice cream has a *swirl* of caramel in it.
Paint the wall with light *swirls*.
A *swirl* of dust rose off the road.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Material made of threads or wires with small open spaces between them.
examples: The screen door is fine wire *mesh*.
Onions come in a plastic *mesh* bag.
The sports shirt has *mesh* panels under the arms.

gloss: A picture or pattern made of many small colored pieces.
examples: The floor of the church is an old *mosaic*.
She made a *mosaic* out of broken tiles.
The museum has Roman *mosaics* from the fourth century.

gloss: A smooth change from one color or shade to another.
examples: The background is a blue *gradient*.
Add a soft *gradient* behind the title.
The poster uses two overlapping *gradients*.

gloss: A pattern or arrangement of lines and shapes made for decoration.
examples: The rug has a simple geometric *design*.
She painted a *design* on the mailbox.
The mugs come in four *designs*.
contrast: The g is silent: dih-ZYNE, never dih-ZIG-n.

gloss: The way the parts of something are arranged on a page or in a space.
examples: I like the *layout* of the front page.
The apartment has an open *layout*.
We tried three different *layouts* before choosing one.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Red, blue, green and so on, or the quality that makes things look that way.
examples: What *color* is your new car?
The garden is full of *color* in June.
The shirt comes in six *colors*.
contrast: American spelling; the British write colour.

gloss: The color of blood and ripe tomatoes.
examples: *Red* is her favorite color.
The painting uses several deep *reds*.
That bright *red* is hard to miss.
contrast: Sounds exactly like read in the past tense, as in I read the book yesterday.

gloss: The color of a clear sky.
examples: The walls are painted a soft *blue*.
He likes dark *blues* and grays.
*Blue* looks good on you.
contrast: Sounds exactly like blew, the past tense of blow.

gloss: The color of grass and leaves.
examples: The kitchen is a pale *green*.
The hills show a dozen shades of *green*.
She mixed two *greens* to get the right tone.

gloss: The color of lemons and school buses.
examples: The front door is a bright *yellow*.
*Yellow* shows dirt easily.
The room is decorated in soft *yellows*.

gloss: The color made by mixing red and blue.
examples: Her bedroom is a deep *purple*.
*Purple* was the color of kings.
The sunset turned through several *purples*.

gloss: A pale red color, like that of many roses.
examples: She painted her nails a bright *pink*.
The sky faded from orange to *pink*.
The catalog shows four different *pinks*.

gloss: The color of chocolate, coffee, or soil.
examples: The couch is a warm *brown*.
The forest is all *browns* and grays in November.
*Brown* hides stains well.

gloss: The darkest color, the opposite of white.
examples: She always wears *black* to work.
The photo is in *black* and white.
The printer is out of *black*.

gloss: The lightest color, like fresh snow.
examples: The trim is painted a clean *white*.
Wash the *whites* separately.
*White* makes the room look bigger.

gloss: The color between black and white, like storm clouds.
examples: The sky was a flat *gray* all day.
He picked a soft *gray* for the hallway.
The paint chips show a dozen *grays*.
contrast: Americans spell it gray; the British spell it grey.

gloss: A pale sandy brown color.
examples: The whole office is painted *beige*.
She wore a coat in soft *beige*.
*Beige* is safe but a little boring.
contrast: Ends in the zh sound of measure, not a hard j: BAYZH.

gloss: A light yellowish brown, or the browner skin color you get from the sun.
examples: He wore *tan* pants and a blue shirt.
She came back from Florida with a deep *tan*.
The store carries the shoe in two *tans*.

gloss: A very dark blue.
examples: He wore a suit in *navy*.
*Navy* goes with almost anything.
The uniform is *navy* with gold buttons.

gloss: A dark brownish red.
examples: The school colors are *maroon* and gold.
She bought a scarf in deep *maroon*.
The seats are covered in *maroon* velvet.

gloss: A deep rich red.
examples: The maple leaves turned a brilliant *crimson*.
She blushed *crimson*.
The banner is *crimson* with white letters.

gloss: A bright red with a slight orange tone.
examples: The cardinal is a flash of *scarlet* in the snow.
She wore *scarlet* to the party.
The poppies were a solid field of *scarlet*.

gloss: A dark blue-green color.
examples: The bathroom tile is a soft *teal*.
I love that jacket in *teal*.
*Teal* looks good next to gray.

gloss: A bright purplish pink.
examples: The printer is low on *magenta*.
The flowers are a shocking *magenta*.
She highlighted the text in *magenta*.

gloss: A deep blue color with a hint of violet.
examples: Real jeans are dyed with *indigo*.
The sky over the desert was pure *indigo*.
The scarf is *indigo* with silver thread.

gloss: A dull yellowish green.
examples: The jacket comes in black or *olive*.
The walls were painted a muddy *olive*.
*Olive* was everywhere in military clothing.

gloss: A dull yellowish brown, often used for uniforms and pants.
examples: He showed up in *khaki* and a polo shirt.
The tent is *khaki* so it blends in.
I keep two pairs of *khakis* for work.
contrast: Americans say KAK-ee; the British say KAH-kee. In the plural, khakis usually means khaki pants.

gloss: A deep purplish red, like red wine.
examples: The couch is a rich *burgundy*.
She chose *burgundy* for the bridesmaid dresses.
His tie is *burgundy* with thin stripes.

gloss: A greenish blue, one of the basic printing colors.
examples: The *cyan* cartridge is empty.
Printers mix *cyan*, magenta, yellow, and black.
The logo is a bright *cyan*.

gloss: A woman or girl with light-colored hair.
examples: She is a natural *blonde*.
Two *blondes* were sitting at the next table.
My sister was a *blonde* until she was ten.
contrast: Blonde with an e usually describes a woman; blond without it is used for men and for hair color in general.

gloss: A woman or girl with dark brown hair.
examples: She was a tall *brunette* in a red coat.
Both *brunettes* were on the swim team.
He always said he preferred *brunettes*.

gloss: A color or shade of color.
examples: The leaves take on a golden *hue* in October.
The painting is full of warm *hues*.
Her face had a greenish *hue*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like hew, meaning to chop with an ax.

gloss: A small amount of a color added to something, making it lighter.
examples: The white paint has a pink *tint*.
The windows have a gray *tint*.
Choose from four *tints* of gray.

gloss: A shade of a color, especially how light or dark it is.
examples: The room is done in warm earth *tones*.
Pick a *tone* that matches your skin.
The photo has a bluish *tone*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A colored substance that gives paint, ink, or skin its color.
examples: The artist grinds his own *pigments*.
Sunlight breaks down the *pigment* in the fabric.
This blue *pigment* was once worth more than gold.

gloss: The range of colors used in a picture or design.
examples: The artist works with a very limited *palette*.
The app lets you save your own color *palettes*.
The film has a cold blue *palette*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like palate, the roof of the mouth, and pallet, a wooden shipping platform.

gloss: How much light something gives off or reflects.
examples: Turn down the *brightness* on your screen.
The *brightness* of the snow hurt my eyes.
You can adjust the *brightness* in the settings.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The difference between light and dark, or a clear difference between two things.
examples: The photo needs more *contrast*.
There is a sharp *contrast* between the two neighborhoods.
The designer likes strong *contrasts* of color.
contrast: The noun is KAHN-trast; the verb, to contrast, is kun-TRAST.

gloss: A soft steady light, or a warm color in someone's face.
examples: A faint *glow* came from under the door.
Her cheeks had a healthy *glow*.
The city gave off an orange *glow* all night.

gloss: The bright look of a smooth clean surface.
examples: The floor has a beautiful *shine*.
Rain took the *shine* right off the car.
Buff the table to bring back its *shine*.

gloss: A smooth shiny finish on a surface.
examples: The paint dries to a high *gloss*.
Her hair had a beautiful *gloss*.
We chose *gloss* rather than flat for the trim.

gloss: A soft gentle shine on a surface.
examples: The silk has a lovely *sheen*.
There was a *sheen* of sweat on his forehead.
Wax gives the wood a warm *sheen*.

gloss: The soft glowing shine of something like a pearl or polished metal.
examples: The old coins have lost their *luster*.
Real pearls have a deep *luster*.
The conditioner brings back the hair's *luster*.
contrast: American spelling; the British write lustre.

gloss: Bright flashing points of light coming off a surface.
examples: The diamond lost none of its *sparkle*.
There was a *sparkle* in her eyes.
Fresh snow has a *sparkle* in the morning sun.

gloss: Tiny shiny pieces used for decoration, or the light they throw off.
examples: The card was covered in gold *glitter*.
There is *glitter* all over the kitchen table.
The dress caught the light with a soft *glitter*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Light that is too bright to look at, or a long angry look.
examples: The *glare* off the water was blinding.
She gave me a cold *glare* and walked away.
The new screen cuts down on *glare*.

gloss: A shape that cannot be seen clearly because its edges are not sharp.
examples: Without my glasses everything is a *blur*.
The car went by in a red *blur*.
The photo shows two gray *blurs* in the background.

gloss: The quality of letting light through so you can see the other side.
examples: The glaze keeps the *transparency* of the glass.
Reduce the *transparency* of that layer.
The plastic loses its *transparency* over time.

gloss: The quality of not letting light through.
examples: Set the *opacity* to fifty percent.
Two coats of paint give better *opacity*.
The fabric has enough *opacity* for a curtain.

gloss: The way someone or something looks.
examples: He cares a lot about his *appearance*.
The house has a neglected *appearance*.
Do not judge people by *appearances*.

gloss: The particular appearance or style of a person or thing.
examples: She has a very natural *look*.
White paint gave the room a fresh *look*.
The band tried out several different *looks*.

gloss: A picture of someone or something, or the way they appear to others.
examples: The company is trying to change its *image*.
Her *image* appeared on the screen.
The book is full of black and white *images*.

gloss: The idea or feeling you get about someone from how they look or act.
examples: He made a good *impression* at the interview.
My first *impression* of the place was terrible.
First *impressions* are hard to change.

gloss: The fact of looking like someone or something else.
examples: There is a strong *resemblance* between the two brothers.
She bears a striking *resemblance* to her grandmother.
The drawing has no *resemblance* to the real building.

gloss: A part of the face, such as the eyes, nose, or mouth.
examples: She has delicate *features*.
His strongest *feature* is his jaw.
The twins share the same *features*.

gloss: The look on someone's face that shows what they feel.
examples: She had a puzzled *expression*.
His *expression* never changed.
The photos catch a whole range of *expressions*.

gloss: An unhappy or worried look made by pulling the eyebrows together.
examples: A deep *frown* crossed his face.
She read the letter with a *frown*.
His *frowns* told me the news was bad.

gloss: The happy look you make by turning up the corners of your mouth.
examples: She greeted us with a warm *smile*.
He gave me a quick *smile* and kept walking.
The kids posed with big *smiles*.

gloss: The general size and shape of a person's body.
examples: He has a slim *build*.
The suspect was of medium *build*.
The brothers have completely different *builds*.

gloss: The shape and condition of a person's body, especially a muscular one.
examples: Years of swimming gave him a powerful *physique*.
She has the *physique* of a dancer.
The magazine is full of impossible *physiques*.
contrast: The ending -que is just a k sound: fih-ZEEK, not fih-ZEE-kwee.

gloss: The way you hold your body when you stand or sit.
examples: Sitting all day is bad for your *posture*.
She has excellent *posture*.
The trainer worked on his *posture* first.

gloss: A person's natural height.
examples: He is small in *stature* but very strong.
Her *stature* made her easy to spot in a crowd.
Jockeys tend to be short in *stature*.

gloss: How tall a person or thing is from bottom to top.
examples: What is your *height* in feet?
The shelf can be set at two *heights*.
The fence is about shoulder *height*.
contrast: Written with -eigh but rhymes with bite, and it ends in a plain t, not th.

gloss: How wide something is from one side to the other.
examples: Measure the *width* of the doorway.
The road narrows to half its usual *width*.
The fabric comes in three *widths*.

gloss: How long something is from end to end.
examples: The table is six feet in *length*.
Cut the rope into four equal *lengths*.
She wants her hair kept at this *length*.

gloss: How deep something is from the top down.
examples: The pool has a *depth* of nine feet at one end.
Check the *depth* of the snow before you drive.
Divers work at *depths* of over a hundred feet.

gloss: How thick something is between its two surfaces.
examples: The wood is about an inch in *thickness*.
Roll the dough to an even *thickness*.
The glass comes in several *thicknesses*.

gloss: How big or small something is.
examples: What *size* shoe do you wear?
The two rooms are about the same *size*.
The shirts come in five *sizes*.

gloss: The way someone's hair is cut and arranged.
examples: She changed her *hairstyle* over the summer.
That *hairstyle* really suits you.
The magazine shows *hairstyles* from the seventies.

gloss: The act of having your hair cut, or the style that results.
examples: I need a *haircut* before the wedding.
Nice *haircut*, by the way.
*Haircuts* are twenty dollars at that place.

gloss: Hair cut straight across the forehead.
examples: She cut her own *bangs* again.
His *bangs* keep falling into his eyes.
I am growing out my *bangs*.
contrast: Americans say bangs and always in the plural; the British call the same thing a fringe.

gloss: Hair tied together at the back of the head so it hangs down.
examples: She pulled her hair back into a *ponytail*.
He runs with his hair in a *ponytail*.
The girls wore matching *ponytails*.

gloss: Hair growing down the sides of a man's face in front of his ears.
examples: He grew long *sideburns* in college.
The barber trimmed his *sideburns*.
Those *sideburns* look very seventies.

gloss: Short hair on a man's face when he has not shaved for a day or two.
examples: He had two days of *stubble* on his chin.
The *stubble* scratched her cheek.
A little *stubble* actually looks good on him.

gloss: A piece of hair that grows or is shaped in a curve.
examples: A loose *curl* fell across her forehead.
The baby has soft blond *curls*.
The rain took the *curl* right out of my hair.

gloss: Hair divided into three parts and woven together.
examples: She wears her hair in a long *braid*.
Mom put my hair in two *braids* for school.
The *braid* came loose during practice.
contrast: Americans say braid; the British usually say plait, pronounced PLAT.

gloss: A small mark that spoils the look of skin or a surface.
examples: The cream is supposed to hide *blemishes*.
The table is perfect except for one small *blemish*.
There was not a single *blemish* on the fruit.

gloss: A thin shallow mark cut into a surface or the skin.
examples: There is a *scratch* on the hood of my car.
The cat left three *scratches* on his arm.
The screen has a tiny *scratch* in the corner.

gloss: A small fault that keeps something from being perfect.
examples: The diamond has one tiny *flaw*.
I could not find a single *flaw* in the finish.
The fabric has a few *flaws* in the weave.

gloss: A long thin line of a different color from what is around it.
examples: She has gray *streaks* in her hair.
There are dirty *streaks* on the window.
A *streak* of light crossed the ceiling.

gloss: A dirty mark made by rubbing something.
examples: There is an ink *smudge* on the last page.
Her glasses were covered in *smudges*.
He wiped the *smudge* off the screen.

gloss: A very small spot or piece of something.
examples: There is a *speck* of dirt on your collar.
*Specks* of paint covered his hands.
The boat was just a *speck* on the horizon.

gloss: A spot or line on a surface that spoils its appearance.
examples: The glass left a ring *mark* on the wood.
There were muddy *marks* all over the floor.
The burn left a small *mark* on her arm.
